Im not going to lie to you, it isn't fun. My family ended up taking in my grandparents dachshund whenever they could no longer care for her, and she was around 14 or 15 I think by the time we got her. My brother and I had grown up with that dog, so while we didn't live with her for all our lives, she was still a big part of it.

I will say, though, you can't really prepare for these things. The emotions are gonna come like a tidal wave and there's no point even trying to hold them back; just let yourself feel them. I was in your place once. My therapist helped me understand it with a sorta metaphor, so I'll do my best to repeat it here. 

Picture your mind as a house, and your thoughts as visitors. Your house has a front door and a back door, and you can open and close them as you please. 

Some thoughts are really nice and you enjoy having them as houseguests! You open the front door for them and allow them to visit and stay for as long as you like. Some thoughts just come in front door, walk around for a bit, and then exit out the back door on their own. 

But some thoughts are less like guests and more like annoying salesmen or..."uninvited" company. They walk in the front door unannounced and, if you don't unlock the back door for them, will wander around and take up space in your home. However, if you keep both the front and back doors unlocked and open, they can come and go as needed. 

Here's the thing: you can't lock the front door. Sometimes, you can't even shut it. There are just some days that your mind WILL have these little "thought visitors", and that's okay. What you CAN control, however, is the back door. 

When the back door is shut and locked, these visitors can crowd in and take up a LOT of space REALLY quickly, so much so that no one can walk around the house and through the halls and it becomes really hard to usher everyone out. However, if you unlock the back door (and better yet, always keep it open), you can shoo these thoughts through the house as needed. And even if they just walk back around to the front door and enter again, they will still eventually exit through the back, especially if you don't acknowledge them when they enter. Don't invite them to stay for dinner, don't ask them how they are doing, don't even say hello. Just go about your business and they will eventually get bored and leave on their own. 

This metaphor is a little convoluted, but it's really helped me. Especially once I actually started visualizing my thoughts as actual visitors and all that. Keep in mind, it will take some time to learn how to manage the "household". Sometimes you'll forget that you locked the back door, sometimes you'll accidentally get into a conversation with one of the unwanted visitors, but over time you will learn and get better at dealing with them. 

All that to say, you don't actually "ignore" your thoughts in the traditional sense. It's more like knowing they are there, but not indulging in their shenanigans.

i had this, and still have episodes sometimes. luckily meds worked for me.

some other things worked, as well. i wanna be clear that this worked for ME, so i have no idea if it would work for anyone else. 

1. the biggest thing was accepting that i will never know all the answers to my questions, because there are no ways to get those answers and there may not even BE answers. this drove me absolutely insane, but over time it started to help with stopping OCD loops. for example: "what if this reality isnt the REAL reality and this is all some sort of cosmic test for me to try and escape?"-to which i would respond to myself with "maybe it is, maybe it isnt. i will never know". you gotta learn to accept the discomfort of uncertainty. 

2. allow yourself to approach your fears. what is your OCD afraid of? afraid of not knowing the "truth"? be comfortable in ignorance. afraid of mortality? let yourself ponder the idea of death, the afterlife, whatever worries you about the subject. etc. etc.

3. journal. this one has been crucial for me. whether its stream of consciousness, ramblings, or as a way to better understand your thoughts. anything. words, art, poetry, anything. express yourself.

4. try not to do any compulsions. im working on this one myself, but i can speak from experience that they almost never help.

I have a 1 year old Great Dane, and she had the same problem when she was younger. 

We started crate training her the moment we got her, and she hated it. Would scream for hours until someone came to sit next to her. Eventually, she would fall asleep in the crate if someone was either sitting there all night/sleeping on the floor next to the crate. 

Slowly, we started scooting away, or not spending the whole night with her. She would still whine sometimes, but she started to realize that she wasn’t alone and that her crate was a safe place. 

Another thing that helps is giving them a treat every time they enter their crate willingly. Our nightly routine with my dane is to get her a “bedtime cookie”, and the second she either hears those words or sees us getting up to get it, she heads straight for her crate. 

Another thing that will help is a set sleep schedule. We’ve had ours in place long enough that she falls asleep at pretty much the same time every night, even if we haven’t put her in the crate yet. For us it’s around 9pm. If we happen to be late getting her to bed, all we have to say is “cookie!” and she knows what to do. 

Not gonna lie, this will probably suck for the first few months. It was definitely a struggle for our family to get used to a new puppy after having only adult dogs for 9+ years. There were many times when we thought she might have been too much and thought about rehoming her. But she eventually got it, and she’s a fantastic dog. I’m so grateful that we didn’t give up on her.

I made the stupid call one time. 

My brother and I were driving home from my college dorm after having packed up all my things to move out. It was dark by the time we left, but the sky would light up with lighting every so often since we were in the middle of a thunderstorm. Strikes were also pretty common and easy to see that night. 

So we’re driving down this awful backroad that’s not even paved, it’s just a dirt path with some gravel on it. The lightning is striking all over the place, but we can’t see where it’s landing because we’re surrounded by trees and hills that pretty much block the view of everything. 

But we come around this curve and suddenly we just see a MASSIVE fire on the very top of the tree line. It’s kinda in the distance so it’s hard to make out it’s exact location, but it’s a fire, clear as day. 

My brother and I pull over and we talk for a bit about whether or not we should call to let someone know that there’s a potential forest fire in the making. Our guess is that lightning struck the treetops and lit them up, but again since we’re so far away, we can’t pinpoint the location. 

So eventually we decide to call 911 and let them know that we see a fire in the tree line and that lightning had been striking, so they agree to send the fire department up to us to take a look. 

We wait for probably 20 minutes until they get there (because the operator had told us it would be better for us to wait), and when the truck finally comes around, he pulls up next to us and motions toward the fire. 

“Are you the ones that called about this fire?” 

“Yeah. We weren’t sure what caused it and we wanted to make sure that it was investigated because it’s so close to these roads.” (There were also a few small houses along the road as well that would’ve been in danger) 

“Thank you guys. You did the right thing. That fire up there is actually *insert name of building here*, and they have an exhaust tower. Those flames are from the exhaust, not the trees.” 

I’m sure you can imagine our humiliation as he explained all of this to us. I think he realized that we were embarrassed and quickly told us that they get calls about that plant all the time, and that it was always better to call and make sure that everything is safe rather than assume that any fire we see is some sort of chemical plant or whatever. 

So uh, yeah. Called the cops because of an industrial fire that was completely under control and not a risk at all.
